name: Anomalocaris canadensis
dietDetails: Preyed upon soft-bodied marine organisms, trilobites, and other Cambrian animals.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Joseph Whiteaves in 1892 in the Burgess Shale.
• Initially its parts were thought to be three separate animals (a shrimp, a jellyfish, and a sponge).
• Reconstructed correctly by Harry Whittington and Derek Briggs in the 1980s.
interestingFacts: ["It was one of the earliest known apex predators, dominating Cambrian seas.","It had highly developed compound eyes with thousands of lenses.","It used flexible lobes on its body sides to swim."]
sizeNotes: Estimated at 1 to 2 kg body mass; length excludes tail filaments.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Anomalocaris canadensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomalocaris%20canadensis"}]

name: Hallucigenia sparsa
dietDetails: Likely fed on organic detritus, sponges, or small animals on the seafloor.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Burgess Shale and first described by Charles Walcott in 1911.
• Simon Conway Morris redescribed it in 1977, famously reconstructing it upside-down and backward.
• Later studies correctly identified its legs and back spines, linking it to modern velvet worms.
interestingFacts: ["Its strange appearance baffled scientists for decades, leading to its name.","It defended itself with rigid pairs of spines along its back.","It belongs to the lobopodians, an ancient group of 'worm-like' animals with legs."]
sizeNotes: Extremely small, ranging from 0.5 to 5.5 cm in length.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Hallucigenia sparsa description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallucigenia%20sparsa"}]

name: Opabinia regalis
nameMeaning: Named after Opabin Pass, British Columbia
dietDetails: Soft-bodied bottom dwellers and organic debris.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Burgess Shale by Charles Walcott in 1912.
• Its bizarre anatomy led to laughter when Harry Whittington presented a reconstruction in 1975.
• It is an important fossil for understanding the early evolution of arthropods.
interestingFacts: ["It had five stalked eyes, granting it a near 360-degree field of vision.","It fed using a flexible, hose-like proboscis tipped with grasping claws.","Unlike many of its contemporaries, it lacked jointed legs, swimming with lateral lobes."]
sizeNotes: Typically 4 to 7 cm in length, excluding the proboscis.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Opabinia regalis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opabinia%20regalis"}]

name: Dunkleosteus terrelli
dietDetails: Fish, sharks, and even smaller Dunkleosteus individuals (cannibalism).
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered by Jay Terrell in 1867 in the Cleveland Shale, Ohio.
• Later named Dunkleosteus in 1956 to honor paleontologist David Dunkle.
• Complete skulls have rarely been found, but its massive armored head plates are iconic.
interestingFacts: ["Instead of teeth, it possessed self-sharpening bony plates that functioned like shears.","It had an incredibly powerful bite, capable of crushing armor-plated prey.","It could open its jaws in a fraction of a second to create a vacuum and suck in prey."]
sizeNotes: Recent studies suggest length estimates might be shorter (around 4.1 meters) due to placoderm body ratios.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Dunkleosteus terrelli description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkleosteus%20terrelli"}]

name: Tiktaalik roseae
dietDetails: Small fish and invertebrates in shallow freshwater streams.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2004 on Ellesmere Island, Canada, by a team led by Neil Shubin.
• Named 'Tiktaalik', meaning 'burbot' in the Inuktitut language, following suggestions from Inuit elders.
• It is considered one of the most significant 'missing links' between fish and land animals.
interestingFacts: ["It possessed primitive wrists and fingers capable of supporting its weight in shallow water.","Unlike typical fish, it had a mobile neck allowing it to turn its head independently.","It had both gills for breathing underwater and lungs for breathing air."]
sizeNotes: Ranged from 1.25 to 2.75 meters (4 to 9 feet) in length.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Tiktaalik roseae description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiktaalik%20roseae"}]

name: Ichthyostega stensioei
nameMeaning: Fish roof (referring to the skull structure)
dietDetails: Fish and large invertebrates found in swampy river deltas.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in East Greenland during an expedition in 1929.
• Described by Gunnar Säve-Söderbergh in 1932.
• Known as one of the first tetrapods in the fossil record, marking the transition to land.
interestingFacts: ["It had seven toes on its hind limbs, showing that early tetrapods did not strictly have five digits.","It likely moved on land similarly to modern mudskippers, pulling itself with front limbs.","Its ribcage was robust, protecting its internal organs when out of the water."]
sizeNotes: Estimated length of 1.5 meters (5 feet). Highly robust body skeleton.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Ichthyostega stensioei description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ichthyostega%20stensioei"}]

name: Arthropleura armata
dietDetails: Decaying vegetation, spores, and lycopsid leaf litter in carboniferous rainforests.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/ca/Arthropleura_NT_small.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Nobu Tamura email:nobu.tamura@yahoo.com  http://spinops.blogspot.com/ http://paleoexhibit.blogspot.com/ (CC BY-SA 4.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AArthropleura_NT_small.jpg"},{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/93/Arthropleura_armata_Palaeontographic57cass_0361.jpg","type":"photo","credit":"Fossil skeletal specimen photo","sourceUrl":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/93/Arthropleura_armata_Palaeontographic57cass_0361.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory:
• Initially described in 1854 based on fragmentary fossils from Germany.
• A massive, nearly complete specimen was found in England in 2018.
• Trackways attributed to it have been found in multiple locations across Europe and North America.
interestingFacts: ["It is the largest known land invertebrate in Earth's history.","Its colossal size was enabled by the high oxygen levels of the Carboniferous atmosphere.","Despite its fearsome appearance, it was a herbivore that fed on rotting plant matter."]
sizeNotes: Ranged from 0.3 to 2.6 meters long; estimated weight up to 50 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Arthropleura armata description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthropleura%20armata"}]

name: Meganeura monyi
dietDetails: Other flying insects, small amphibians, and early reptiles.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in the coal measures of Commentry, France, in 1880.
• Described by Charles Brongniart in 1885.
• Further discoveries have cemented its status as one of the largest flying insects ever.
interestingFacts: ["It is closely related to modern dragonflies but belongs to an extinct group called griffinflies.","Its wingspan could reach over 70 centimeters (28 inches).","It was an agile aerial predator that hunted other insects and possibly small amphibians."]
sizeNotes: Wingspan: 65 to 71 cm; body length: ~43 cm. Weight estimates range from 100 to 200 grams.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Meganeura monyi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meganeura%20monyi"}]

name: Dimetrodon grandis
dietDetails: Fish, amphibians, and other reptiles like Eryops and Edaphosaurus.
discoveryHistory:
• Named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1878 during the 'Bone Wars'.
• Abundant fossils have been excavated from the Red Beds of Texas.
• It is one of the most thoroughly studied of all early synapsids.
interestingFacts: ["Though often confused with dinosaurs, it lived millions of years earlier and is closer to mammals.","Its iconic sail was likely used for thermoregulation or mating displays.","It had two distinct types of teeth in its jaws, a trait common to later mammals."]
sizeNotes: Ranged from 1.7 to 4.6 meters long across various species; D. grandis was one of the largest.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Dimetrodon grandis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimetrodon%20grandis"}]

name: Edaphosaurus pogonias
dietDetails: Tough terrestrial plants, horsetails, and ferns, crushed with its specialized tooth plates.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in Texas and described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1882.
• One of the first large, terrestrial herbivores known to science.
• Notable for its highly specialized feeding apparatus compared to contemporary predators.
interestingFacts: ["It possessed a large sail supported by vertebral spines featuring unique crossbars.","Its mouth was filled with peg-like teeth forming plates for crushing tough plants.","It had a disproportionately small head compared to its massive, barrel-shaped body."]
sizeNotes: Ranged from 1 to 3.5 meters in length. Weight reached up to 300 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Edaphosaurus pogonias description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edaphosaurus%20pogonias"}]

name: Helicoprion bessonowi
dietDetails: Soft-bodied cephalopods like ammonites and belemnites.
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Alexander Karpinsky in 1899 from Russian fossils.
• The exact placement of its bizarre tooth whorl debated for over a century.
• A 2013 CT scan of a specimen finally confirmed the whorl fit within its lower jaw.
interestingFacts: ["It retained old teeth, curling them into a spiral instead of shedding them.","It belongs to the eugenodonts, a group of cartilaginous fish closer to ratfish than true sharks.","Its jaw mechanism sliced through soft-bodied prey like a circular saw."]
sizeNotes: Estimates range from 5 to 8 meters (16 to 26 feet) based on tooth whorl proportions.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Helicoprion bessonowi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helicoprion%20bessonowi"}]

name: Scutosaurus karpinskii
dietDetails: Low-lying plants, shrubs, and roots in dry, arid environments.
discoveryHistory:
• Found by Vladimir Amalitsky near the Northern Dvina River in Russia in the 1890s.
• Named posthumously in 1921.
• It represents one of the most specialized and armored pareiasaurs discovered.
interestingFacts: ["Its body was covered in bony plates called osteoderms for defense.","It walked with its legs positioned more vertically under its body, unusual for Permian reptiles.","It had a massive ribcage to house a large digestive tract for processing fibrous plants."]
sizeNotes: Grew up to 3 meters (10 feet) long, weighing around 1 metric ton.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Scutosaurus karpinskii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scutosaurus%20karpinskii"}]

name: Inostrancevia alexandri
nameMeaning: Named after Russian geologist Aleksandr Inostrantsev
dietDetails: Large herbivores like Scutosaurus and dicynodonts.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in northern Russia by Vladimir Amalitsky in the late 19th century.
• Described formally in 1922.
• In 2023, fossils were found in South Africa, demonstrating a vast geographic range.
interestingFacts: ["It was the largest of the gorgonopsians, early predatory relatives of mammals.","It wielded massive saber-like canine teeth for hunting large, thick-skinned prey.","It could open its jaws incredibly wide to utilize its impressive fangs."]
sizeNotes: Total length reached up to 3.5 meters (11.5 feet), with a skull length of 50 cm.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Inostrancevia alexandri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inostrancevia%20alexandri"}]

name: Coelophysis bauri
dietDetails: Preyed on small reptiles and cynodonts.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by E.D. Cope in 1887 in New Mexico.
interestingFacts: ["Early agile theropod.", "Mass bonebeds at Ghost Ranch.", "Hollow thin-walled bones."]
sources: [{"citation": "Cope, E.D. (1887). Trans. Amer. Phil. Soc.", "url": "https://doi.org/10.2307/1005527"}]

name: Plateosaurus trossingensis
dietDetails: High foliage, cycads, and conifers, processed with leaf-shaped teeth.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1834 near Nuremberg, Germany, by Johann Engelhardt. Described by Hermann von Meyer in 1837.
interestingFacts: {"An early sauropodomorph, a group that would eventually evolve into the giant, long-necked sauropods.","Strictly bipedal; its hands were unable to rotate, making quadrupedal walking anatomically impossible.","Fossil mass graves in Europe suggest they traveled in herds or became trapped in mud flats."}
sizeNotes: Highly variable adult sizes, ranging from 4.8 to 10 meters in length and 600 to 4,000 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"von Meyer, H. (1837). Original description of Plateosaurus trossingensis.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38670"},{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Plateosaurus spp. description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateosaurus"}]

name: Postosuchus kirkpatricki
dietDetails: Apex predator hunting dicynodonts.
discoveryHistory: Named by Sankar Chatterjee in 1985.
interestingFacts: ["Apex rauisuchian predator.", "Deep skull with dagger teeth.", "Semi-bipedal posture."]
sources: [{"citation": "Chatterjee, S. (1985). Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. B.", "url": "https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rstb.1985.0002"}]

name: Dilophosaurus wetherilli
dietDetails: Preyed upon fish, small dinosaurs, and early herbivorous reptiles.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Northern Arizona by Jesse Williams in 1942. Named Dilophosaurus in 1970 by Samuel Paul Welles.
interestingFacts: {"Made famous by Jurassic Park, but the real animal was much larger, did not spit venom, and lacked a neck frill.","The twin crests on its skull were paper-thin and likely used for species recognition and courtship displays.","Its jaw was loosely connected near the front, which may have allowed it to catch fish or hook prey."}
sizeNotes: Grew up to 6 meters (20 feet) long, weighing about 400 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Welles, S.P. (1954). New Jurassic dinosaur from the Kayenta formation of Arizona. Bulletin of the Geological Society of America 65: 591–598.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38641"},{"citation":"Marsh, A.D. and Rowe, T.B. (2020). A comprehensive anatomical revision of Dilophosaurus wetherilli. Journal of Paleontology 94(S78): 1–60.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1017/jpa.2020.14"}]

name: Stegosaurus stenops
nameMeaning: Roof lizard with a narrow face
dietDetails: Low-lying plants, mosses, ferns, horsetails, and cycads.
discoveryHistory: First found in Colorado in 1877 by M.P. Felch. Described by Othniel Charles Marsh during the famous Bone Wars.
interestingFacts: {"Had 17 flat bony plates on its back that were not used for armor but likely for display or temperature regulation.","Its tail weapon, consisting of 4 long spikes, is formally called a 'thagomizer' (a term coined in a Far Side cartoon).","Its brain was famously tiny, about the size of a walnut, weighing only 80 grams."}
sizeNotes: Large individuals reached up to 9 meters in length and up to 7 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Marsh, O.C. (1887). Principal characters of American Jurassic dinosaurs. Part IX. The Stegosauria. American Journal of Science 34: 413–417.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38810"},{"citation":"Maidment, S.C.R. et al. (2008). Systematics and phylogeny of Stegosauria. Journal of Systematic Palaeontology 6(4): 367–407.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1017/S1477201908002459"}]

name: Brachiosaurus altithorax
nameMeaning: Arm lizard with a deep chest
dietDetails: High canopy conifers, ginkgos, and tree ferns.
discoveryHistory: First discovered in the Grand River Valley, Colorado, by Elmer Riggs in 1900. Described in 1903.
interestingFacts: {"Its front legs were longer than its hind legs, giving its back a sloping profile similar to a giraffe.","Unlike other sauropods, it held its neck nearly vertically to reach high-altitude vegetation.","Had massive, chisel-like teeth to crop leaves from tall branches without chewing them."}
sizeNotes: Length estimates range from 18 to 22 meters; weight ranges from 28 to 58 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Riggs, E.S. (1903). Brachiosaurus altithorax, the largest known dinosaur. American Journal of Science 15(88): 299–306.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38685"},{"citation":"Taylor, M.P. (2009). A re-evaluation of Brachiosaurus altithorax Riggs 1903 (Dinosauria: Sauropoda). Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology 29(3): 787–806.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1671/039.029.0301"}]

name: Allosaurus fragilis
dietDetails: Medium to large herbivorous dinosaurs like Stegosaurus and sauropods.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/55/Allosaurus_BW_mirrored.jpg","type":"art","credit":"Rlevente, original author: Nobu Tamura (CC BY-SA 4.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AAllosaurus_BW_mirrored.jpg"},{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fe/Allosaurus_Jaws_Steveoc86.jpg","type":"photo","credit":"Fossil jaw specimen photo","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Allosaurus_Jaws_Steveoc86.jpg"}]
discoveryHistory: First described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877 based on fragmentary remains from Colorado. Dozens of individuals were later found at the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in Utah.
interestingFacts: {"The most common large predator of Late Jurassic North America, accounting for a vast majority of theropod fossils found.","Its skull was highly flexible and could expand laterally, allowing it to swallow large chunks of meat.","Had a lower bite force than modern lions, suggesting it used its skull like an axe to slash at prey."}
sizeNotes: Average length was 8.5 meters (28 feet), but rare large specimens (like Saurophaganax) reached 11-12 meters.
sources: [{"citation":"Marsh, O.C. (1877). Notice of new dinosaurian reptiles from the Jurassic formation. American Journal of Science 14: 514–516.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38596"}]

name: Archaeopteryx lithographica
nameMeaning: Ancient wing from the lithographic limestone
dietDetails: Insects, small lizards, and early mammals.
discoveryHistory: First fossil (a single feather) discovered in 1860 in the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, Germany. The famous London Specimen was found in 1861.
interestingFacts: {"Famous transitional fossil representing the link between non-avian theropod dinosaurs and modern birds.","Had flight feathers like a bird, but retained reptilian features: a long bony tail, three clawed fingers, and a jaw with teeth.","Its discovery occurred just two years after Charles Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species', serving as key evidence."}
sizeNotes: Roughly the size of a modern common raven or magpie, weighing 0.5 to 1.0 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"von Meyer, H. (1861). Archaeopteryx lithographica aus dem lithographischen Schiefer von Solnhofen. Neues Jahrbuch für Mineralogie, Geognosie, Geologie und Petrefaktenkunde: 678–679.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=39327"}]

name: Yi qi
dietDetails: Small vertebrates, insects, and soft plant matter in forest canopies.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by a farmer in Hebei Province, China. Described in 2015 by Xu Xing and colleagues.
interestingFacts: {"Had bat-like wings made of a membranous skin stretched between long fingers and a unique bony rod (styliform element).","One of the smallest known non-avian dinosaurs, adapting to an arboreal, gliding lifestyle.","Its plumage preserved melanosomes, suggesting it had black and brown coloration."}
sizeNotes: Wingspan was around 60 cm; weighed roughly 380 grams.
sources: [{"citation":"Xu, X. et al. (2015). A bizarre Jurassic theropod dinosaur with membranous wings. Nature 521(7550): 70–73.","url":"https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14423"}]

name: Tyrannosaurus rex
dietDetails: Apex predator preying on large herbivores like Triceratops and Edmontosaurus.
discoveryHistory: First discovered by Arthur Lakes in Colorado (1874), later named and described by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1905.
interestingFacts: {"Had one of the strongest bite forces among all terrestrial animals, estimated at 35,000 to 57,000 Newtons.","Its tiny two-clawed arms were surprisingly strong, capable of lifting around 200 kilograms each.","Whether it had feathers is still debated, though direct fossil impressions show predominantly scaly skin."}
sizeNotes: Estimates range from 8,400 to 14,000 kg depending on study.
sources: [{"citation":"Osborn, H.F. (1905). Tyrannosaurus and other Cretaceous carnivorous dinosaurs. Bulletin of the AMNH 21(14): 259–265.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38613"}]

name: Triceratops horridus
dietDetails: Low-growing vegetation like ferns, cycads, and palms, cropped with its powerful beak.
discoveryHistory: First found near Denver, Colorado, in 1887 by George Lyman Cannon. Described by Othniel Charles Marsh.
interestingFacts: {"The large frill and three horns were likely used for defense against predators and in courtship or dominance displays.","Its skull was one of the largest of any land animal, reaching up to 2.5 meters in length.","Lived alongside Tyrannosaurus rex, and fossil bones show healed T. rex bite marks, proving they clashed."}
sizeNotes: Estimates range from 6,000 to 12,000 kg depending on body mass calculations.
sources: [{"citation":"Marsh, O.C. (1889). Notice of new American dinosaurs. American Journal of Science 37(220): 331–336.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38861"}]

name: Velociraptor mongoliensis
dietDetails: Protoceratops and small desert tetrapods.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Peter Kaisen in 1923 at Flaming Cliffs.
interestingFacts: ["Retractable 9 cm sickle claw on second toe.", "Quill knobs on ulna proving presence of feathers.", "Slender upturned snout."]
sources: [{"citation": "Osborn, H.F. (1924). Amer. Mus. Novit.", "url": "https://hdl.handle.net/2246/3221"}]

name: Parasaurolophus walkeri
dietDetails: High and low vegetation, conifers, leaves, and twigs, processed with grinding dental batteries.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Alberta, Canada, in 1920 by William Parks. Described in 1922.
interestingFacts: {"The hollow, curved crest on its head functioned as a resonating chamber to produce low-frequency vocalizations.","Could walk on both two legs (when running or browsing) and four legs (when slow walking or grazing).","Its crest was also likely used for visual display and species identification."}
sizeNotes: Grew to about 9.5 meters long; weight estimated at 2.5 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Parks, W.A. (1922). Parasaurolophus walkeri, a new genus and species of crested trachodont dinosaur. University of Toronto Studies, Geological Series 13: 1–32.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38776"}]

name: Ankylosaurus magniventris
nameMeaning: Fused lizard with a great belly
dietDetails: Low-growing plants, ferns, and shrubs, cropped with its broad beak.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in the Hell Creek Formation of Montana by Barnum Brown in 1906. Described in 1908.
interestingFacts: {"Had a heavy armor of bony osteoderms and a massive bony club at the end of its tail, used for self-defense.","The tail club was supported by fused vertebrae, allowing it to deliver bone-shattering blows to attackers.","Lived in the same environments as Tyrannosaurus rex, serving as one of its most heavily fortified prey."}
sizeNotes: Ranged from 6 to 8 meters long; weighed roughly 5 to 8 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Brown, B. (1908). The Ankylosauridae, a new family of armored dinosaurs from the Upper Cretaceous. Bulletin of the AMNH 24(12): 187–201.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38827"}]

name: Carnotaurus sastrei
dietDetails: Medium-sized herbivores and small dinosaurs in open dry landscapes.
discoveryHistory: Found in Chubut Province, Argentina, by Anselmo Sastre in 1984 during an expedition led by José Bonaparte.
interestingFacts: {"Possessed two distinct, thick horns above its eyes, unique among carnivorous dinosaurs.","Its forelimbs were vestigial, even smaller than those of T. rex, and lacked claws entirely.","Had extremely fast leg muscles, making it one of the fastest running large theropods known."}
sizeNotes: Ranged from 7.5 to 9 meters in length; weight is estimated around 1.35 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Bonaparte, J.F. (1985). A horned Cretaceous carnosaur from Patagonia, Carnotaurus sastrei n.g. et n.sp. OS Museum Novitates: 1–16.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38602"}]

name: Quetzalcoatlus northropi
nameMeaning: Named after the Aztec feathered serpent god Quetzalcoatl
dietDetails: Small vertebrates, carrion, and terrestrial prey.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Big Bend National Park, Texas, by Douglas A. Lawson in 1971. Described in 1975.
interestingFacts: {"The largest known flying animal in Earth's history, with a wingspan comparable to a small private airplane.","When standing on the ground, it was as tall as a modern giraffe (around 5.5 meters).","Likely hunted on land by stalking prey on all fours, similar to modern marabou storks."}
sizeNotes: Wingspan: 10 to 11 meters; weight estimates range from 70 to 250 kg due to light, air-filled bones.
sources: [{"citation":"Lawson, D.A. (1975). Pterosaur from the Latest Cretaceous of West Texas: Discovery of the Largest Flying Creature. Science 187(4180): 947–948.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38507"}]

name: Pteranodon longiceps
dietDetails: Fishes, squids, and small marine organisms caught by diving.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1870 in the Smoky Hill Chalk of Kansas. It was the first pterosaur found outside Europe.
interestingFacts: {"Unlike earlier pterosaurs, it lacked teeth and had a bird-like beak.","Males had a large, backward-pointing crest on their skull, likely used for display and steering.","Fossils suggest they spent most of their time gliding over the Western Interior Seaway."}
sizeNotes: Wingspan: 5.6 meters for females, up to 7.2 meters for males. Weight: ~30 to 90 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Marsh, O.C. (1876). Notice of new Odontornithes and Pterosauria. American Journal of Science 11(66): 507–509.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=38499"}]

name: Mosasaurus hoffmannii
dietDetails: Fish, ammonites, sharks, plesiosaurs, sea turtles, and even smaller mosasaurs.
discoveryHistory: First found in a chalk quarry near Maastricht, Netherlands, in 1764. The skull became famous when French revolutionary forces confiscated it in 1794.
interestingFacts: {"Not a dinosaur, but a giant marine reptile closely related to modern monitor lizards and snakes.","Had a second row of teeth (pterygoid teeth) on the roof of its mouth, preventing prey from escaping down its throat.","Propelled itself through water with a powerful, shark-like tail fin, using its flippers only for steering."}
sizeNotes: Large specimens reached up to 15 to 17 meters in length; weight is estimated at 10 to 15 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Mantell, G.A. (1829). A tabular view of the osseous remains of reptiles in the South-East of England. Transactions of the Geological Society of London 2(3): 421–424.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=36399"}]

name: Elasmosaurus platyurus
nameMeaning: Thin-plate lizard with a flat tail
dietDetails: Small bony fish, squids, and shelled cephalopods.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Kansas in 1867 by Theophilus Turner. Described by Edward Drinker Cope, who notoriously reconstructed the fossil with the head on the tail end.
interestingFacts: {"Had an extremely long neck consisting of 72 neck vertebrae, more than any other known animal.","Its neck was relatively rigid and could not be bent like a snake; it likely swam slowly beneath fish schools and darted its head up.","Swallowed small pebbles (gastroliths) to help grind food and control its buoyancy."}
sizeNotes: Total length was 10.3 meters (34 feet), of which 7.1 meters was the neck.
sources: [{"citation":"Cope, E.D. (1868). Remarks on a new enaliosaurian, Elasmosaurus platyurus. Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia 20: 92–93.","url":"https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=36440"}]

name: Gastornis parisiensis
dietDetails: Tough plant material, nuts, seeds, and fruit, crushed using its massive bill.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1855 near Paris by Gaston Planté.
• Known for a long time under the synonym 'Diatryma' in North America.
• Once thought to be a top predator, modern analysis of its remains indicates it was herbivorous.
interestingFacts: ["Despite its intimidating beak, isotopic evidence suggests it fed on tough plants and seeds.","It was completely flightless but possessed strong, muscular legs.","It lived in dense forests during the warm climate of the early Eocene."]
sizeNotes: Grew up to 2 meters (6.6 feet) tall; weight ranged from 150 to 200 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Gastornis parisiensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastornis%20parisiensis"}]

name: Basilosaurus cetoides
nameMeaning: King lizard (named before its whale nature was known)
dietDetails: Fish, sharks, and smaller marine mammals like Dorudon.
discoveryHistory:
• Initial discoveries in the US were so common the bones were used as fireplace supports.
• Described initially as a giant reptile ('king lizard') by Richard Harlan in 1834.
• Richard Owen correctly identified it as an early whale in 1839.
interestingFacts: ["It was a primitive whale that maintained tiny, non-functional hind legs.","Its body was unusually elongated and serpentine compared to modern whales.","It could not echolocate and relied on good eyesight and hearing to hunt."]
sizeNotes: Elongated body shape. Length: 15 to 20 meters. Weight: ~5 to 7 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Basilosaurus cetoides description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilosaurus%20cetoides"}]

name: Megalodon
dietDetails: Large marine mammals, baleen whales, seals, sirenians, and sea turtles.
discoveryHistory:
• Its fossilized teeth were originally thought to be the petrified tongues of dragons.
• Nicolas Steno correctly identified them as shark teeth in 1667.
• Louis Agassiz gave it the scientific name meaning 'giant tooth' in 1843.
interestingFacts: ["It was the largest predatory shark known to have existed.","Because its skeleton was made of cartilage, primarily only its teeth and vertebrae fossilized.","It preyed heavily on small whales, and its extinction coincided with a cooling climate."]
sizeNotes: Estimates range from 15 to 20 meters (50 to 65 feet); weight estimates range from 30 to 65 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Otodus megalodon description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megalodon"}]

name: Smilodon fatalis
dietDetails: Large herbivores like bison, camels, horses, and ground sloths.
discoveryHistory:
• Described by Joseph Leidy in 1869 from fossils found in Texas.
• Thousands of skeletons have been recovered from the La Brea Tar Pits in California.
• It is arguably the most famous extinct mammal aside from the woolly mammoth.
interestingFacts: ["Its iconic saber teeth could reach up to 7 inches in length.","It had a weaker bite force than a modern lion but robust forelimbs to pin prey.","Its jaws could open up to 120 degrees to clear its massive fangs for a bite."]
sizeNotes: Length: 1.75 meters (excluding short tail); height: 1.0 meter at shoulder. Weight: 160 to 280 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Smilodon fatalis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smilodon%20fatalis"}]

name: Mammuthus primigenius
dietDetails: Grasses, sedges, shrubs, and herbaceous plants in the mammoth steppe.
discoveryHistory:
• Scientifically described by Johann Friedrich Blumenbach in 1799.
• Spectacular mummified remains have been found preserved in the Siberian permafrost.
• Known from extensive interactions with early humans, documented in cave art.
interestingFacts: ["It had a specialized double coat of hair and a thick layer of fat for insulation.","Its ears were much smaller than those of modern elephants to prevent heat loss.","Its massive, curved tusks were likely used to sweep away snow to reach vegetation."]
sizeNotes: Males stood 2.7 to 3.4 meters tall at the shoulder; females were smaller. Weight: 4 to 6 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Mammuthus primigenius description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammuthus%20primigenius"}]

name: Megatherium americanum
dietDetails: Leaves, twigs, and shrubs; could stand on hind legs to reach high branches.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in Argentina in 1788 by Manuel Torres.
• Described by the famous naturalist Georges Cuvier in 1796.
• It was one of the first prehistoric mammals to be reconstructed and exhibited.
interestingFacts: ["It was a giant ground sloth that reached the size of an elephant.","It possessed massive claws used for stripping leaves from branches, not for hunting.","It could rear up on its hind legs, using its heavy tail as a tripod for balance."]
sizeNotes: Total length reached up to 6 meters (20 feet) from head to tail; weighed around 4 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Megatherium americanum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megatherium%20americanum"}]

name: Coelodonta antiquitatis
dietDetails: Grasses, sedges, and woody tundra vegetation.
discoveryHistory:
• First formally described by Johann Friedrich Blumenbach in 1799.
• Numerous mummified specimens have been found frozen in Siberia.
• Perfectly preserved specimens have even been found in oil seeps in Poland.
interestingFacts: ["It was a large, woolly rhinoceros adapted to the cold Pleistocene environment.","It had a massive, flattened front horn used for clearing snow from the ground.","It is frequently depicted in Paleolithic European cave paintings."]
sizeNotes: Grew up to 3.8 meters (12 feet) in length; stood 2.0 meters tall. Weight: ~1.8 to 2.7 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Coelodonta antiquitatis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coelodonta%20antiquitatis"}]

name: Doedicurus clavicaudatus
nameMeaning: Pestle tail (referring to the tail club)
dietDetails: Low-growing grasses, herbs, and wetland plants.
discoveryHistory:
• Described by Richard Owen in 1874 from fossils found in Argentina.
• It is one of the best-known members of the glyptodont family.
• Early humans coexisted with it and may have hunted it for meat and its large shell.
interestingFacts: ["It was a massive relative of the armadillo, heavily armored with a bony carapace.","It defended itself with a spiked, club-like tail reminiscent of a medieval mace.","Its rigid shell meant it could not roll into a ball like some modern armadillos."]
sizeNotes: Total length was 4.0 meters; shell height was 1.5 meters. Weighed about 1.4 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Doedicurus clavicaudatus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doedicurus%20clavicaudatus"}]

name: Thylacoleo carnifex
dietDetails: Large marsupials like Diprotodon and giant kangaroos.
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Richard Owen in 1859 from fragmented remains.
• A nearly complete skeleton discovered in 2002 offered unprecedented insight into its anatomy.
• Known from fossils across the Australian continent.
interestingFacts: ["It is the largest known carnivorous marsupial from Australia.","It had massive, blade-like premolars designed to shear through meat and bone.","It featured a unique, semi-opposable thumb claw to grapple with large prey."]
sizeNotes: Stood 75 cm at shoulder; length 1.5 meters. Weighed 90 to 130 kg, comparable to a small female lion.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Thylacoleo carnifex description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thylacoleo%20carnifex"}]

name: Diprotodon optatum
dietDetails: Shrubs, twigs, leaves, and saltbush in dry, open woodlands.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in the Wellington Caves of New South Wales in the 1830s.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1838.
• Trackways reveal they moved in large herds across the Australian interior.
interestingFacts: ["It is the largest marsupial ever discovered, comparable in size to a rhinoceros.","Like modern wombats, females had a backward-facing pouch.","It migrated vast distances in search of water and food during the Pleistocene."]
sizeNotes: Length: ~3.8 meters; height at shoulder: 2.0 meters. Weighed up to 2.8 metric tons.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Diprotodon optatum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diprotodon%20optatum"}]

name: Lisowicia
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Triassic beds.
• First described by renowned paleontologists.
• Holotype specimen includes cranial and postcranial elements.
• Subject to various taxonomic revisions over time.
interestingFacts: ["One of the apex organisms of its ecosystem.","Displays unique morphological adaptations for its era.","Fossils have contributed significantly to our understanding of the Triassic.","It coexisted with early dinosaurs and other archosaurs."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Lisowicia spp. description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisowicia"}]

• Described by George H. Baur in 1887.
• Represents one of the most common early ichthyosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["A transitional ichthyosaur with a straight tail.","Retained a distinct neck, unlike later forms.","Small and agile marine predator."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Mixosaurus spp. description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixosaurus"}]

name: Besanosaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered at the Besano formation in Italy in 1993.
• Described by Dal Sasso and Pinna in 1996.
• The holotype specimen was pregnant.
interestingFacts: ["A large shastasaurid ichthyosaur.","Lacked a dorsal fin.","Gave birth to live young tail-first, like modern cetaceans."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Besanosaurus spp. description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Besanosaurus"}]

name: Shastasaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in Mount Shasta, California.
• Described by Merriam in 1895.
• Later found in China and Canada.
interestingFacts: ["One of the largest marine reptiles ever.","S. sikanniensis reached over 20 meters in length.","Likely a suction feeder lacking typical teeth."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Shastasaurus spp. description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shastasaurus"}]

name: Guanlingsaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in Guanling County, Guizhou, China.
• Described by Yin et al. in 2000.
• Often considered a species of Shastasaurus.
interestingFacts: ["Characterized by a uniquely short and toothless snout.","An enormous marine reptile.","Adapted for suction feeding on soft-bodied cephalopods."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Guanlingsaurus spp. description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanlingsaurus"}]

name: Eudimorphodon
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered near Bergamo, Italy in 1973.
• Described by Rocco Zambelli.
• One of the oldest known pterosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed complex, multi-cusped teeth.","Had a diamond-shaped flap of skin at the end of its long tail.","Likely a piscivore (fish-eater)."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Eudimorphodon spp. description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eudimorphodon"}]

name: Preondactylus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Preone valley in Italy in 1982.
• Described by Rupert Wild in 1984.
• Specimen was discovered in a piece of bituminous limestone.
interestingFacts: ["One of the most basal pterosaurs.","Had single-cusped teeth unlike Eudimorphodon.","Wingspan was less than half a meter."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Preondactylus spp. description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preondactylus"}]

name: Austriadactylus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in the 20th century.
interestingFacts: ["Austriadactylus is an important Triassic species.","It tells us about early ecosystems."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Austriadactylus spp. description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austriadactylus"}]

name: Caviramus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in the 20th century.
interestingFacts: ["Caviramus is an important Triassic species.","It tells us about early ecosystems."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Caviramus spp. description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caviramus"}]

name: Ceratosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Described by O.C. Marsh in 1884 based on a nearly complete skeleton from Colorado.
• A notable specimen was found in the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry.
• Fossils have been discovered in North America, with possible remains in Portugal and Tanzania.
interestingFacts: ["It had a prominent horn on its snout.","Ceratosaurus possessed osteoderms along its back.","It likely competed with Allosaurus for prey."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Ceratosaurus nasicornis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceratosaurus"}]

name: Megalosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• The first genus of non-avian dinosaur to be validly named (1824 by William Buckland).
• Early discoveries in Oxfordshire, England, were initially interpreted as giant lizards.
• It became a 'wastebasket taxon' in the 19th and 20th centuries for many unclassified theropods.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'Great Lizard'.","It was one of the original three genera used to define 'Dinosauria'.","True Megalosaurus fossils are only known from the Middle Jurassic of England."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Megalosaurus bucklandii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megalosaurus"}]

name: Cryolophosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1990-91 during a field expedition in Antarctica led by William Hammer.
• Officially named in 1994, it was the first meat-eating dinosaur found in Antarctica.
• Additional material was recovered during subsequent expeditions in the 2000s.
interestingFacts: ["Known as 'Elvisaurus' due to its pompadour-like crest.","It lived in a relatively temperate Antarctic climate.","It is the largest known Early Jurassic theropod."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Cryolophosaurus ellioti description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryolophosaurus"}]

name: Monolophosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1981 by a Canadian-Chinese expedition in Xinjiang, China.
• Described and named in 1993 by Zhao Xijin and Philip J. Currie.
• The holotype is a nearly complete skeleton with an articulated skull.
interestingFacts: ["It had a single large crest running down the midline of its snout.","The crest was heavily pneumatized (hollow).","It lived in an environment with deep lakes and rivers."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Monolophosaurus jiangi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monolophosaurus"}]

name: Torvosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1972 by Jim Jensen and Kenneth Stadtman in Colorado.
• Described in 1979 by Peter Galton and Jensen.
• A second species, T. gurneyi, was later identified from Portugal.
interestingFacts: ["It was one of the largest predators of its time.","It had exceptionally powerful jaws and large teeth.","Torvosaurus competed with Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus in the Morrison Formation."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Torvosaurus tanneri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torvosaurus"}]

name: Ornitholestes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1900 at the Bone Cabin Quarry in Wyoming.
• Described by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1903.
• Only one nearly complete skeleton is known.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'bird robber'.","It was a small, fast, and agile predator.","Contrary to early restorations, it likely did not have a horn on its nose."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Ornitholestes hermanni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornitholestes"}]

name: Compsognathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• The first specimen was discovered in the 1850s in the Solnhofen limestone of Germany.
• A larger, second specimen was found in France in 1971.
• It was historically considered the smallest known dinosaur for over a century.
interestingFacts: ["It was a very small, bipedal carnivore.","Its fossils were found with the remains of small lizards in their stomachs.","It lived on an archipelago in a shallow tropical sea."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Compsognathus longipes description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compsognathus"}]

name: Guanlong
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2000 in the Junggar Basin, Xinjiang, China.
• Named in 2006 by Xu Xing and colleagues.
• Two specimens, an adult and a juvenile, were found together.
interestingFacts: ["It is one of the earliest known tyrannosauroids.","It possessed a large, fragile crest on its head.","Its name means 'crowned dragon'."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Guanlong wucaii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanlong"}]

name: Proceratosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1910 in Gloucestershire, England.
• Initially thought to be an ancestor of Ceratosaurus (hence the name) when described in 1926.
• In 2010, it was reclassified as an early tyrannosauroid.
interestingFacts: ["It possessed a small crest on its snout.","It is one of the oldest known members of the tyrannosaur lineage.","Only a partial skull has been found."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Proceratosaurus bradleyi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proceratosaurus"}]

name: Metriacanthosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the 19th century in the Oxford Clay of England.
• Originally classified as a species of Megalosaurus in 1923.
• Alick Walker established the genus Metriacanthosaurus in 1964.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'moderately-spined lizard'.","It had tall neural spines on its back, though not forming a full sail.","It was a medium-sized apex predator of its ecosystem."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Metriacanthosaurus parkeri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metriacanthosaurus"}]

name: Eustreptospondylus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in 1871 in a clay pit near Oxford, England.
• It was shuffled between several genera, including Megalosaurus, before Alick Walker named it in 1964.
• It remains one of the most complete theropod skeletons found in Europe.
interestingFacts: ["It lived in an island environment.","It may have scavenged marine carcasses that washed ashore.","The single known specimen is considered a subadult."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Eustreptospondylus oxoniensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eustreptospondylus"}]

name: Piatnitzkysaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1977 by José Bonaparte in the Cañadón Asfalto Formation, Argentina.
• Described in 1979 as an early allosauroid or megalosauroid.
• Two partial skeletons are known.
interestingFacts: ["It was a medium-sized bipedal predator.","It represents one of the few known Middle Jurassic theropods from South America.","It shares primitive traits with basal tetanurans."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Piatnitzkysaurus floresi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piatnitzkysaurus"}]

name: Marshosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1976 at the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in Utah.
• Named by James Madsen in 1976 in honor of O.C. Marsh.
• Known from sparse, fragmentary remains.
interestingFacts: ["It was a medium-sized predator in the Morrison Formation.","It was rarer than competitors like Allosaurus.","Its exact taxonomic position within tetanurans is debated."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Marshosaurus bicentesimus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshosaurus"}]

name: Stokesosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1974 at the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry, Utah.
• Named by James Madsen after geologist William Lee Stokes.
• Primarily known from a pair of distinct ilia (pelvic bones).
interestingFacts: ["It is an early member of the tyrannosauroid family.","It was a small, agile predator.","Similar fossils found in England were later reclassified as a separate genus, Juratyrant."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Stokesosaurus clevelandi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stokesosaurus"}]

name: Tanycolagreus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1995 at the Bone Cabin Quarry West in Wyoming.
• Originally thought to be Coelurus, it was named as a new genus in 2005.
• The holotype includes a nearly complete skull and skeleton.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'long-limbed hunter'.","It was slightly larger and more robust than its relative Ornitholestes.","It had a long, low skull compared to other small theropods."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Tanycolagreus topwilsoni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanycolagreus"}]

name: Sciurumimus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in a limestone quarry in Bavaria, Germany.
• Described in 2012 by Oliver Rauhut and colleagues.
• The single specimen is an exceptionally preserved juvenile.
interestingFacts: ["The fossil preserves filamentous feathers, especially along the tail.","Its name means 'squirrel mimic' due to its bushy tail.","Initially thought to be a megalosauroid, it may be a primitive coelurosaur."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Sciurumimus albersdoerferi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sciurumimus"}]

name: Juravenator
dietDetails: Typical diet for a theropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1998 in the Solnhofen limestone in Germany.
• Named in 2006 by Ursula Göhlich and Luis Chiappe.
• The specimen is a nearly complete juvenile skeleton.
interestingFacts: ["Its fossil shows patches of scaly skin, suggesting a lack of feathers in some areas.","It had unusually large eyes, suited for nocturnal hunting.","It was a very small, agile predator."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Juravenator starki description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juravenator"}]

name: Diplodocus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1877 in Colorado by Benjamin Mudge and Samuel Williston.
• Described by O.C. Marsh in 1878.
• The famous 'Dippy' cast is based on a specimen found in 1899 in Wyoming.
interestingFacts: ["It had an exceptionally long, whip-like tail.","Its center of gravity allowed it to rear up on its hind legs.","Its teeth were peg-like and restricted to the front of the jaw."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Diplodocus carnegii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplodocus"}]

name: Apatosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered and named by O.C. Marsh in 1877 in Colorado.
• For over a century, its skeleton was mounted with the wrong skull (that of a Camarasaurus).
• A correct skull was finally mounted on skeletons in the late 1970s.
interestingFacts: ["It had a very robust, heavily built skeleton compared to Diplodocus.","Its tail may have been able to crack like a whip, producing a loud sound.","It was an abundant herbivore in the Morrison Formation."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Apatosaurus ajax description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apatosaurus"}]

name: Brontosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Named by O.C. Marsh in 1879 from a specimen found at Como Bluff, Wyoming.
• In 1903, it was synonymized with Apatosaurus and the name fell out of formal use.
• A comprehensive study in 2015 reinstated Brontosaurus as a valid, separate genus.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'thunder lizard'.","It had a slightly thinner and less robust neck than Apatosaurus.","It is one of the most culturally famous dinosaur names."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Brontosaurus excelsus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brontosaurus"}]

name: Camarasaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1877 in Colorado by Oramel W. Lucas.
• Named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1877.
• It is the most common sauropod found in the Morrison Formation.
interestingFacts: ["It had a boxy, blunt skull with large, spoon-shaped teeth.","Its name means 'chambered lizard', referring to hollow chambers in its vertebrae.","It likely fed on tough, fibrous vegetation."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Camarasaurus supremus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camarasaurus"}]

name: Giraffatitan
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tendaguru Formation in Tanzania between 1909 and 1912.
• Originally described as a species of Brachiosaurus (B. brancai) in 1914 by Werner Janensch.
• Elevated to its own genus, Giraffatitan, by Gregory S. Paul in 1988.
interestingFacts: ["It is one of the tallest known dinosaurs.","A famous, nearly complete skeleton is mounted in the natural history museum in Berlin.","It was adapted for high-browsing on conifer trees."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Giraffatitan brancai description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giraffatitan"}]

name: Barosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by early bone hunters for O.C. Marsh in South Dakota in 1889.
• Named in 1890, though more complete remains were found later in Utah.
• Remains have also been controversially attributed to it from Tanzania.
interestingFacts: ["It is closely related to Diplodocus but had a significantly longer neck.","Its neck vertebrae were exceptionally elongated.","A famous mount at the AMNH shows it rearing up to defend against an Allosaurus."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Barosaurus lentus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barosaurus"}]

name: Dicraeosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered during the German Tendaguru expeditions in Tanzania (1909–1912).
• Described by Werner Janensch in 1914.
• Multiple specimens have been recovered, making it well-understood.
interestingFacts: ["It had tall, bifurcated (Y-shaped) neural spines on its neck and back.","It had a relatively short neck for a sauropod.","It was a low-browser in an ecosystem dominated by taller sauropods."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Dicraeosaurus hansemanni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dicraeosaurus"}]

name: Omeisaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1939 in Sichuan, China.
• Named by C.C. Young in 1939 after Mount Omei.
• Massive bonebeds in the Dashanpu Quarry have yielded numerous skeletons.
interestingFacts: ["It had a long, heavily built neck.","Some species assigned to it may have had a tail club.","It was a common large herbivore in its ecosystem."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Omeisaurus junghsiensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omeisaurus"}]

name: Vulcanodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1969 on an island in Lake Kariba, Zimbabwe.
• Described by Michael Raath in 1972.
• Originally thought to be a prosauropod due to associated carnivore teeth, later recognized as scavenged.
interestingFacts: ["It is one of the earliest known true sauropods.","Its forelimbs retained some primitive traits while its hindlimbs were column-like.","It lived in a volcanic landscape."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Vulcanodon karibaensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcanodon"}]

name: Patagosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the 1970s in the Cañadón Asfalto Formation, Argentina.
• Described by José Bonaparte in 1979.
• Remains of at least six individuals were found together, suggesting gregarious behavior.
interestingFacts: ["It was a basal eusauropod with a relatively short neck.","Adults and juveniles were found together, indicating herd living.","It was a dominant herbivore in its South American ecosystem."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Patagosaurus fariasi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patagosaurus"}]

name: Cetiosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in England and named by Richard Owen in 1841.
• It was the very first sauropod ever discovered and named.
• Originally, Owen believed it was a giant marine crocodile, hence the name 'whale lizard'.
interestingFacts: ["Its vertebrae lacked the complex hollow air sacs seen in later sauropods.","It was a primitive sauropod weighing roughly 15 tons.","It serves as an important baseline for understanding early sauropod evolution."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Cetiosaurus oxoniensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cetiosaurus"}]

name: Spinophorosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2006 in Niger by a Spanish-German expedition.
• Described in 2009 by Remes and colleagues.
• The holotype is one of the most complete basal sauropod skeletons ever found.
interestingFacts: ["It originally was thought to have a spiked tail club (thagomizer), but the spikes were later re-identified as collarbones.","It is one of the best-preserved early sauropods.","Its anatomy provides a crucial link between basal sauropodomorphs and eusauropods."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Spinophorosaurus nigerensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinophorosaurus"}]

name: Haplocanthosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1901 by William H. Utterback in Colorado.
• Named by John Bell Hatcher in 1903.
• Known from a few incomplete specimens in the Morrison Formation.
interestingFacts: ["It is considered a primitive macronarian sauropod.","It lacked the extreme specialized features of Diplodocus or Camarasaurus.","It was one of the smaller sauropods of the Morrison Formation."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Haplocanthosaurus priscus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplocanthosaurus"}]

name: Supersaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1972 by Jim Jensen at the Dry Mesa Quarry in Colorado.
• Named in 1985 based on massive, isolated bones.
• More complete remains found in Wyoming in 1996 confirmed its distinct genus status.
interestingFacts: ["It is among the longest dinosaurs ever discovered.","It was a diplodocid, closely related to Apatosaurus.","Its neck vertebrae were exceptionally elongated and robust."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Supersaurus vivianae description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersaurus"}]

name: Suuwassea
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1999 in Montana by a University of Pennsylvania expedition.
• Named in 2004 by J.D. Harris and Peter Dodson.
• The name comes from a Native American word meaning 'ancient thunder'.
interestingFacts: ["It is a primitive member of the dicraeosaurid family.","It possessed an extra opening (foramen) in its skull of unknown function.","It provides evidence for early diplodocoid radiation in North America."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Suuwassea emilieae description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suuwassea"}]

name: Jobaria
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1997 by Paul Sereno's expedition in the Sahara Desert, Niger.
• Described in 1999 based on numerous well-preserved skeletons.
• The dating of its formation is debated, ranging from Middle Jurassic to Early Cretaceous.
interestingFacts: ["It had a relatively short, primitive neck compared to later sauropods.","Its spoon-shaped teeth were adapted for nipping branches.","It was the most common large herbivore in its African environment."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Jobaria tiguidensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jobaria"}]

name: Bellusaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a sauropod of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Junggar Basin in Xinjiang, China.
• Described in 1987 by Dong Zhiming.
• Seventeen juvenile skeletons were found together in a single quarry.
interestingFacts: ["The mass grave suggests a herd perished together in a flash flood.","All known specimens are juveniles.","It was a small macronarian sauropod."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Bellusaurus sui description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellusaurus"}]

name: Dryosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1876 in Wyoming and sent to O.C. Marsh.
• Described by Marsh in 1894, meaning 'oak lizard' due to leaf-shaped teeth.
• Skeletons of multiple growth stages have been found.
interestingFacts: ["It was a fast, agile bipedal runner.","It lacked the thumb spikes seen in later iguanodonts.","It was a highly successful, small herbivore of the Morrison Formation."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Dryosaurus altus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dryosaurus"}]

name: Camptosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1879 by William Harlow Reed in Wyoming.
• Named by O.C. Marsh in 1885.
• It is commonly found in association with Stegosaurus remains.
interestingFacts: ["It was a heavily built ornithopod that could walk on two or four legs.","It possessed a small, hooved thumb on its hands.","Its beak was toothless, but it had tightly packed cheek teeth."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Camptosaurus dispar description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camptosaurus"}]

name: Kentrosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered during the German expeditions to the Tendaguru Formation, Tanzania (1909–1912).
• Described by Edwin Hennig in 1915.
• Hundreds of bones were excavated, allowing for detailed reconstruction.
interestingFacts: ["Its back was covered in pairs of plates that transitioned into long spikes near the tail.","It featured a prominent spike pointing backward from each shoulder.","It was smaller and more primitively built than Stegosaurus."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Kentrosaurus aethiopicus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentrosaurus"}]

name: Scutellosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1971 in the Kayenta Formation, Arizona.
• Described in 1981 by E.H. Colbert.
• Hundreds of small osteoderms (armor plates) were found with the skeleton.
interestingFacts: ["It is one of the earliest known armored dinosaurs.","It was a small, lightly built, bipedal herbivore.","Its body was covered in parallel rows of small bony scutes."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Scutellosaurus lawleri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scutellosaurus"}]

name: Scelidosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1858 at Charmouth, England, by James Harrison.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1861.
• Exceptionally complete specimens have been recovered from marine deposits.
interestingFacts: ["It was covered in rows of keeled bony armor.","It is considered an early relative of both ankylosaurs and stegosaurs.","It was a quadrupedal browser with a small head and leaf-shaped teeth."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Scelidosaurus harrisonii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scelidosaurus"}]

name: Gargoyleosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1996 in the Bone Cabin Quarry West, Wyoming.
• Named in 1998 by Ken Carpenter and colleagues.
• The holotype includes a nearly complete, well-preserved skull.
interestingFacts: ["It is one of the earliest and most complete known ankylosaurs.","Its heavily armored skull had prominent horns on the rear corners.","It had a complex network of nasal passages."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Gargoyleosaurus parkpinorum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gargoyleosaurus"}]

name: Othnielosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the late 19th century and heavily revised over time.
• Named in 2007 by Peter Galton to replace the confused taxon Othnielia.
• Known from several partial skeletons in the Morrison Formation.
interestingFacts: ["It was a small, swift, bipedal herbivore.","It possessed enameled teeth well-adapted to chewing tough vegetation.","Its name honors paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Othnielosaurus consors description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Othnielosaurus"}]

name: Lesothosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in Lesotho in the upper Elliot Formation.
• Described by Peter Galton in 1978.
• The holotype includes partial skull and postcranial material.
• Originally thought to be an ornithopod, later recognized as a basal ornithischian.
interestingFacts: ["One of the earliest known ornithischian dinosaurs.","It had a small, slender body built for fast running.","Its teeth were leaf-shaped, adapted for slicing plant material."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Lesothosaurus diagnosticus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesothosaurus"}]

name: Hexinlusaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Fossils found in the Lower Shaximiao Formation, China.
• Described originally as a species of Yandusaurus in 1983.
• Reclassified and named Hexinlusaurus by Barrett et al. in 2005.
• Name honors Professor He Xinlu.
interestingFacts: ["A small, basal neornithischian dinosaur.","It had prominent ridges on its teeth for grinding.","Coexisted with larger dinosaurs like Shunosaurus."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Hexinlusaurus multidens description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexinlusaurus"}]

name: Chialingosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Upper Shaximiao Formation in Sichuan, China in 1957.
• Described by C.C. Young in 1959.
• One of the first stegosaurs discovered in China.
• The holotype is based on fragmentary remains.
interestingFacts: ["It was a very slender and primitive stegosaur.","Named after the Jialing River in Sichuan.","Its plates were narrower and more spine-like compared to later stegosaurs."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Chialingosaurus kuani description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chialingosaurus"}]

name: Tuojiangosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Upper Shaximiao Formation of Sichuan, China in 1977.
• Described by Dong Zhiming and colleagues.
• Best-known Asian stegosaur, with a nearly complete skeleton.
• Named after the Tuo River.
interestingFacts: ["Featured 15 pairs of pointed plates along its back.","Had a distinctive pair of spikes on its shoulders.","Bore a thagomizer with four large spikes at the end of its tail."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Tuojiangosaurus multispinus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuojiangosaurus"}]

name: Dacentrurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in England in 1874.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1875, originally as Omosaurus.
• Renamed Dacentrurus in 1902 by Frederic Lucas.
• Was the very first stegosaur ever discovered.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed paired spikes rather than plates along most of its back and tail.","Its front limbs were relatively long for a stegosaur.","The pelvis was exceptionally broad to accommodate a large gut."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Dacentrurus armatus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacentrurus"}]

name: Miragaia
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Lourinhã Formation, Portugal.
• Described by Octávio Mateus and colleagues in 2009.
• The holotype consists of the front half of a skeleton, notably the neck.
• Named after the Portuguese parish of Miragaia.
interestingFacts: ["Had an unusually long neck with at least 17 vertebrae.","Its neck length rivaled some sauropods.","Its back was adorned with paired triangular plates."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Miragaia longicollum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miragaia"}]

name: Hesperosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Wyoming, USA, in 1985.
• Described by Kenneth Carpenter in 2001.
• The holotype includes a nearly complete skull and much of the skeleton.
• Its name means western lizard.
interestingFacts: ["Closely related to Stegosaurus but had broader, oval-shaped plates.","Its skull was proportionately wider than that of Stegosaurus.","Lived slightly earlier than most Stegosaurus species."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Hesperosaurus mjosi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hesperosaurus"}]

name: Fruitadens
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA, in the 1970s.
• Described by Richard Butler and colleagues in 2010.
• The name means Fruita tooth, after the Fruita Paleontological Area.
• Represented by remains of multiple individuals.
