interestingFacts: ["One of the smallest known ornithischian dinosaurs.","Had canine-like tusks in its lower jaw.","Likely an omnivore, eating both plants and small animals or insects."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Fruitadens haagarorum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fruitadens"}]

name: Nanosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a ornithischian of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA.
• Described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877.
• Historically a taxonomic wastebasket taxon.
• Recent studies have clarified its classification among early ornithischians.
interestingFacts: ["A small, agile, bipedal dinosaur.","Othnielosaurus is often considered a synonym of Nanosaurus.","Used speed to escape from contemporary predators like Allosaurus."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Nanosaurus agilis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanosaurus"}]

name: Rhamphorhynchus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Bavaria, Germany.
• First named by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1847.
• Known from numerous perfectly preserved specimens.
• Many specimens preserve soft tissues, including wing membranes.
interestingFacts: ["Had a long, stiff tail ending in a diamond-shaped vane.","Its jaws were filled with sharp, forward-pointing teeth for catching fish.","Lacked a bony crest on its head."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Rhamphorhynchus muensteri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhamphorhynchus"}]

name: Dimorphodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Dorset, England, in 1828.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1859.
• One of the first pterosaurs ever found.
• Name means two-form tooth, referring to its differentiated teeth.
interestingFacts: ["Had a remarkably large, deep skull resembling that of a puffin.","Possessed two distinct types of teeth in its jaws.","Its wings were relatively short, suggesting it was not an oceanic soarer."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Dimorphodon macronyx description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimorphodon"}]

name: Pterodactylus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Bavaria, Germany.
• Described by Cosimo Alessandro Collini in 1784.
• The first pterosaur ever identified as a flying reptile.
• Georges Cuvier later coined the name Ptero-dactyle.
interestingFacts: ["Had a long, pointed beak filled with small teeth.","It was a short-tailed pterosaur (pterodactyloid).","Likely fed on small fish and invertebrates."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Pterodactylus antiquus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pterodactylus"}]

name: Anurognathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• Described by Ludwig Döderlein in 1923.
• The holotype is a small, nearly complete skeleton on a single slab.
• Its name means without tail and jaw.
interestingFacts: ["Had a very short skull and broad, frog-like mouth.","Unlike its relatives, it had a very short tail.","Likely an aerial insectivore, similar to modern nightjars."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Anurognathus ammoni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anurognathus"}]

name: Scaphognathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• First described by August Goldfuss in 1831.
• Originally assigned to Pterodactylus before getting its own genus.
• Only a few specimens have ever been found.
interestingFacts: ["Had a broader, more robust skull than its relative Rhamphorhynchus.","Its teeth were vertically oriented rather than pointing forward.","Its brain was relatively large compared to other early pterosaurs."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Scaphognathus crassirostris description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scaphognathus"}]

name: Sordes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Karabastau Formation of Kazakhstan in 1971.
• Described by Aleksandr Grigorevich Sharov.
• The holotype prominently preserved impressions of hair-like structures (pycnofibers).
• The name Sordes pilosus means hairy devil.
interestingFacts: ["Provided the first undeniable proof that pterosaurs were covered in fluff.","Had a thick coat of pycnofibers over its body and part of its wings.","Was a small, long-tailed pterosaur."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Sordes pilosus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sordes"}]

name: Darwinopterus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation, Liaoning, China.
• Described by Lü Junchang and colleagues in 2009.
• Named in honor of Charles Darwin on the 200th anniversary of his birth.
• Represented by numerous complete skeletons, including one with an egg.
interestingFacts: ["A crucial missing link showing modular evolution in pterosaurs.","Had a long tail like early pterosaurs, but the skull of advanced ones.","Exhibited clear sexual dimorphism, with males having head crests."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Darwinopterus modularis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darwinopterus"}]

name: Wukongopterus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation, Liaoning, China.
• Described by Wang Xiaolin and colleagues in 2009.
• Named after Sun Wukong, the Monkey King from Chinese mythology.
• The holotype is a nearly complete skeleton.
interestingFacts: ["Part of the transitional group connecting basal and advanced pterosaurs.","Had a robust tail and elongated cervical vertebrae.","Likely arboreal, navigating through dense forest environments."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Wukongopterus lii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wukongopterus"}]

name: Kunpengopterus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation of China.
• Described by Wang Xiaolin and colleagues in 2010.
• Named after the Kunpeng, a mythical Chinese creature that transforms from fish to bird.
• Known from well-preserved specimens including an egg.
interestingFacts: ["Recently discovered to possess an opposable thumb.","The opposable thumb suggests it lived and climbed in trees.","It lacked a bony crest on its head."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Kunpengopterus sinensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunpengopterus"}]

name: Ctenochasma
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• Described by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1852.
• Its name means comb jaw.
• Found primarily in late Jurassic marine deposits.
interestingFacts: ["Had hundreds of long, thin teeth forming a comb-like structure.","Used its unique jaws to filter-feed on small aquatic organisms.","Was a fully flying equivalent to modern flamingos."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Ctenochasma roemeri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ctenochasma"}]

name: Gnathosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• Described by Hermann von Meyer in 1833.
• Was originally mistaken for a teleosaurid (marine crocodile).
• Reidentified as a pterosaur by Albert Oppel in 1862.
interestingFacts: ["Its jaws broadened at the tip into a spoon-like shape.","Possessed over 130 needle-like teeth.","Fed by sweeping its jaws through mud to catch small invertebrates."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Gnathosaurus subulatus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gnathosaurus"}]

name: Cycnorhamphus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone in Germany.
• First named in 1855, but later lumped with Pterodactylus.
• Reinstated as a distinct genus in the mid-20th century.
• Name means swan beak.
interestingFacts: ["Had unusual jaws with a distinctive upward curve or kink.","Likely used its specialized jaws to crush hard-shelled prey.","Lacked teeth in the front portion of its mouth."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Cycnorhamphus suevicus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycnorhamphus"}]

name: Germanodactylus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
• Originally assigned to Pterodactylus in 1901.
• Reclassified as its own genus by C.C. Young in 1964.
• Name means German finger.
interestingFacts: ["Had a prominent bony crest running along the top of its skull.","Its jaws were mostly toothless at the very front.","Likely hunted fish, similar to modern terns."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Germanodactylus cristatus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanodactylus"}]

name: Pterorhynchus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Daohugou Beds of Inner Mongolia, China.
• Described by Stephen Czerkas and Ji Qiang in 2002.
• Only one well-preserved specimen has been found.
• The name means wing snout.
interestingFacts: ["Preserved an intricate, sail-like crest made of keratin.","Had long hair-like pycnofibers with distinct tufts.","Its tail vane was reinforced by elongated scales."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Pterorhynchus wellnhoferi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pterorhynchus"}]

name: Harpactognathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Wyoming, USA.
• Described by Kenneth Carpenter and colleagues in 2003.
• Known only from a partial snout.
• Name means snatching jaw.
interestingFacts: ["One of the few large pterosaurs known from the Morrison Formation.","Had a significant bony crest extending to the tip of its snout.","Its wingspan is estimated to have been around 2.5 meters."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Harpactognathus gentryii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpactognathus"}]

name: Mesadactylus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA.
• Described by James Jensen and Kevin Padian in 1989.
• Known from fragmentary remains, primarily a synsacrum.
• Name means Mesa finger, after the discovery site at Dry Mesa Quarry.
interestingFacts: ["One of the earliest recognized pterodactyloid pterosaurs in North America.","Was quite small, with an estimated wingspan under 1 meter.","Its isolated bones were initially confused with bird remains."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Mesadactylus ornithosphyos description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesadactylus"}]

name: Jianchangnathus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation, Liaoning, China.
• Described by Xin Cheng and colleagues in 2012.
• The holotype is a nearly complete skeleton.
• Closely related to the genus Scaphognathus.
interestingFacts: ["Had a highly robust lower jaw with a prominent chin.","Only three teeth were present in each maxilla.","Its tail was relatively straight and rigid."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Jianchangnathus robustus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jianchangnathus"}]

name: Fenghuangopterus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a pterosaur of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning, China.
• Described by Lü Junchang and colleagues in 2010.
• Represented by a single, beautifully preserved skeleton.
• Named after the Fenghuang, a mythological Chinese bird.
interestingFacts: ["A member of the scaphognathine group of pterosaurs.","Had a blunt, short skull packed with vertically oriented teeth.","Provides key insights into early pterosaur diversity in Asia."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Fenghuangopterus lii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenghuangopterus"}]

name: Liopleurodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation, England or France.
• Described by Henri Émile Sauvage in 1873.
• Name means smooth-sided tooth, referring to its tooth enamel.
• Gained fame through its exaggerated depiction in Walking with Dinosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["A formidable apex predator of the Jurassic seas.","Though famously portrayed as 25 meters long, it actually reached about 6-7 meters.","Had an exceptionally powerful bite force."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Liopleurodon ferox description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liopleurodon"}]

name: Plesiosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Lyme Regis, England, in 1823.
• Described by William Conybeare in 1824.
• The first complete plesiosaur skeleton ever found.
• Its name means near lizard.
interestingFacts: ["Characterized by a small head, long neck, and four large flippers.","Moved through the water by flying with its flippers, like modern sea turtles.","Its diet consisted mainly of fish and small cephalopods."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Plesiosaurus dolichodeirus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plesiosaurus"}]

name: Ichthyosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Lyme Regis, England, in the early 19th century.
• Described by Charles König in 1818.
• The first fully recognized genus of the ichthyosaur group.
• Its name translates to fish lizard.
interestingFacts: ["Convergent evolution gave it a body shape strikingly similar to a modern dolphin.","Gave birth to live young at sea, as proven by fossilized mothers with embryos.","Had massive eyes reinforced by bony rings for deep-water vision."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Ichthyosaurus communis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ichthyosaurus"}]

name: Ophthalmosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation of England.
• Described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1874.
• Hundreds of specimens have been discovered worldwide.
• The name means eye lizard.
interestingFacts: ["Had the largest eyes relative to body size of any known vertebrate.","Its enormous eyes suggest it hunted in deep, dark waters.","Possessed a teardrop-shaped body built for high-speed swimming."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Ophthalmosaurus icenicus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ophthalmosaurus"}]

name: Cryptoclidus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation, England.
• Described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1892.
• Name means hidden collarbone, referring to its small clavicles.
• Known from numerous excellent skeletons.
interestingFacts: ["Had a surprisingly fragile skull for a marine predator.","Its jaws were lined with dozens of interlocking, needle-like teeth.","Likely fed by trapping small fish and soft-bodied squid."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Cryptoclidus eurymerus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptoclidus"}]

name: Rhomaleosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Alum Shale Formation of Yorkshire, England.
• Described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1874.
• The most famous specimen is named the Barrow Kipper.
• Name means strong lizard.
interestingFacts: ["A large, robust pliosaur with a powerful build.","Had an internal nasal passage that allowed it to smell underwater.","Hunted other large marine reptiles as well as big fish."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Rhomaleosaurus cramptoni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhomaleosaurus"}]

name: Macroplata
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Blue Lias Formation in Warwickshire, England.
• Described by William Elgin Swinton in 1930.
• The holotype includes a nearly complete skeleton.
• Its name means big plate, referring to its large shoulder bones.
interestingFacts: ["Had an unusually long neck for an early pliosaur.","Its skull was robust and crocodilian in shape.","Reached about 4.5 meters in length."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Macroplata tenuiceps description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macroplata"}]

name: Peloneustes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation of England.
• Described by Richard Lydekker in 1889.
• The name translates roughly to mud swimmer.
• Known from numerous specimens.
interestingFacts: ["A relatively small pliosaur, measuring around 3 meters long.","Had fewer, more robust teeth than its relatives.","Specialized in hunting hard-shelled prey like ammonites and belemnites."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Peloneustes philarchus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peloneustes"}]

name: Pliosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in the Kimmeridge Clay Formation of England.
• Described by Richard Owen in 1841.
• It is the type genus for the entire group of short-necked plesiosaurs.
• The famous Predator X was eventually classified as a species of Pliosaurus.
interestingFacts: ["An enormous apex predator of the Late Jurassic.","Its skull could reach over 2 meters in length.","Its bite force was powerful enough to crush a car."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Pliosaurus brachydeirus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliosaurus"}]

name: Simolestes
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation of England in the 19th century.
• Described by Charles William Andrews in 1909.
• Name means snub-nosed thief.
• A very complete skeleton was found in a brick pit in Peterborough.
interestingFacts: ["Had a remarkably short, blunt snout.","Its jaw muscles were exceptionally large, giving it a very powerful bite.","Likely specialized in twisting chunks of flesh off large prey."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Simolestes vorax description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simolestes"}]

name: Temnodontosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by Mary Anning in Lyme Regis, England.
• Described by Richard Lydekker in 1889.
• The first ichthyosaur skull ever found belonged to this genus.
• Name means cutting-tooth lizard.
interestingFacts: ["One of the largest known ichthyosaurs, reaching up to 12 meters.","An apex predator that fed on other marine reptiles and large cephalopods.","Possessed large, robust teeth with distinct cutting edges."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Temnodontosaurus platyodon description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temnodontosaurus"}]

name: Excalibosaurus
dietDetails: Typical diet for a marine reptile of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Lower Lias of Somerset, England, in 1984.
• Described by Christopher McGowan in 1986.
• Named after Excalibur, King Arthur legendary sword.
• Known from a nearly complete skeleton.
interestingFacts: ["Like Eurhinosaurus, it had an extremely elongated upper jaw.","Its front flippers were much shorter than those of its relatives.","Helps document the evolutionary transition of swordfish-like ichthyosaurs."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Excalibosaurus costini description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibosaurus"}]

name: Morganucodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in limestone fissures in Glamorgan, Wales, in 1941.
• Described by Walter Kühne in 1949.
• Its name means Glamorgan tooth.
• Thousands of isolated teeth and bones have since been found.
interestingFacts: ["One of the earliest and most transitional forms between cynodonts and true mammals.","Had a double jaw joint, a hallmark of early mammalian evolution.","Was a tiny, shrew-like animal that hunted insects at night."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Morganucodon watsoni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morganucodon"}]

name: Castorocauda
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Daohugou Beds of Inner Mongolia, China, in 2004.
• Described by Qiang Ji and colleagues in 2006.
• Preserved remarkably detailed impressions of hair and soft tissue.
• Name means beaver tail.
interestingFacts: ["The earliest known mammal-like animal with a beaver-like tail and webbed feet.","Provides evidence that early mammaliaforms were highly specialized, not just generalized shrews.","Preserves the oldest known evidence of mammalian hair."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Castorocauda lutrasimilis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castorocauda"}]

name: Volaticotherium
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Daohugou Beds of Inner Mongolia, China.
• Described by Jin Meng and colleagues in 2006.
• The fossil excellently preserved a large gliding membrane.
• Name means ancient gliding beast.
interestingFacts: ["The earliest known gliding mammal-like animal.","Pushed back the origin of mammalian gliding flight by 70 million years.","Had sharp teeth adapted for a purely insectivorous diet."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Volaticotherium antiquum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volaticotherium"}]

name: Fruitafossor
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Morrison Formation of Colorado, USA, in 2005.
• Described by Zhe-Xi Luo and John Wible.
• Named after the town of Fruita, Colorado, and fossor meaning digger.
• Nicknamed Popeye due to its massive arm bones.
interestingFacts: ["Had remarkably strong forelimbs adapted for digging, like a modern mole or aardvark.","Its tube-like, rootless teeth were perfectly suited for eating colonial insects like termites.","Shows that early mammals were highly ecologically diverse."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Fruitafossor windscheffeli description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fruitafossor"}]

name: Juramaia
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning, China.
• Described by Zhe-Xi Luo and colleagues in 2011.
• The fossil preserves a nearly complete skull and skeleton with soft tissue traces.
• Name means Jurassic mother from China.
interestingFacts: ["The earliest known eutherian (placental) mammal.","Pushed back the divergence date of placental and marsupial mammals by 35 million years.","Its forelimbs indicate it was an agile tree climber."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Juramaia sinensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juramaia"}]

name: Agilodocodon
dietDetails: Typical diet for a early mammal of its size.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation in Inner Mongolia, China.
• Described by Qing-Jin Meng and colleagues in 2015.
• Represented by an incredibly well-preserved skeleton.
• Name means agile docodont.
interestingFacts: ["An early mammaliaform that was highly adapted for living in trees.","Its teeth suggest it had a specialized diet of tree sap.","Possessed highly flexible wrists and elbows for grasping branches."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Agilodocodon scansorius description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agilodocodon"}]

name: Giganotosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1993 by Rubén Darío Carolini in Patagonia, Argentina.
• Formally named Giganotosaurus carolinii in 1995 by Coria and Salgado.
• Additional fragments of a potentially larger individual were found in later years.
interestingFacts: ["It had highly serrated teeth ideal for slicing flesh.","Possessed an elongated skull with an underdeveloped sense of smell compared to T. rex.","Likely preyed on giant titanosaur sauropods."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Giganotosaurus carolinii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giganotosaurus"}]

name: Deinonychus
dietDetails: Pack hunter
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1931 by Barnum Brown in Montana.
• John Ostrom redefined our understanding of dinosaurs by describing it in 1969.
• Ostrom's study of Deinonychus sparked the 'Dinosaur Renaissance'.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'terrible claw', referring to the large sickle claw on its foot.","Provided crucial evidence for the evolutionary link between dinosaurs and birds.","Often found in groups, suggesting possible pack-hunting behavior."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Deinonychus antirrhopus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinonychus"}]

name: Albertosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1884 by Joseph Burr Tyrrell in Alberta, Canada.
• Named Albertosaurus in 1905 by Henry Fairfield Osborn.
• A massive bonebed containing over 20 individuals was found in 1910.
interestingFacts: ["The bonebed discovery suggests it may have lived and hunted in packs.","Was lighter and faster than the closely related Tyrannosaurus rex.","Grew at a rapid pace, reaching mature size in less than 20 years."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Albertosaurus sarcophagus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albertosaurus"}]

name: Utahraptor
dietDetails: Large prey
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1991 by a team led by James Kirkland in Utah.
• Officially named Utahraptor ostrommaysi in 1993.
• Additional specimens have since been found trapped in a potential quicksand predator trap.
interestingFacts: ["The largest known member of the dromaeosaurid family.","Its massive sickle claw could reach up to 9.4 inches in length.","Built for power rather than speed, unlike smaller raptors."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Utahraptor ostrommaysi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utahraptor"}]

name: Oviraptor
dietDetails: Opportunist
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1923 by George Olsen during an expedition to Mongolia.
• Named 'egg thief' because the first fossil was found atop a clutch of eggs.
• Later discoveries proved the eggs belonged to Oviraptor itself, and it was brooding them.
interestingFacts: ["Had a short, parrot-like beak with no teeth.","Likely possessed a crest on its head, similar to a modern cassowary.","Its brooding posture strongly resembles that of modern birds."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Oviraptor philoceratops description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oviraptor"}]

name: Majungasaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1896 by a French military officer in Madagascar.
• Originally named Megalosaurus crenatissimus by Charles Depéret in 1896.
• A complete skull discovered in 1996 clarified its classification as an abelisaurid.
interestingFacts: ["Provides the first unambiguous evidence of dinosaur cannibalism.","Had a distinctive dome on its skull, unique among theropods.","Possessed robust, muscular hind legs but very short arms."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Majungasaurus crenatissimus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majungasaurus"}]

name: Baryonyx
dietDetails: Piscivore
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1983 by amateur fossil hunter William Walker in Surrey, England.
• Described in 1986 by Alan Charig and Angela Milner.
• The holotype specimen included fish scales in its stomach region.
interestingFacts: ["Had a long, narrow snout resembling that of a crocodile.","Its large thumb claw was likely used to hook fish out of water.","Represents one of the earliest known spinosaurid dinosaurs."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Baryonyx walkeri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baryonyx"}]

name: Acrocanthosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the early 1940s in Oklahoma, USA.
• Named Acrocanthosaurus atokensis in 1950 by Stovall and Langston.
• A nearly complete skeleton 'Fran' was discovered in the 1990s.
interestingFacts: ["Characterized by tall neural spines along its back and neck.","Likely the apex predator of the Early Cretaceous in North America.","Its tracks have been found alongside those of giant sauropods in Texas."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Acrocanthosaurus atokensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acrocanthosaurus"}]

name: Dromaeosaurus
dietDetails: Small prey
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1914 by Barnum Brown in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta.
• Named by Brown and Matthew in 1922.
• The type species of the family Dromaeosauridae.
interestingFacts: ["Had a heavily built skull with a stronger bite force than Velociraptor.","Relied on its jaws rather than its claws to kill prey.","Was one of the first 'raptor' dinosaurs discovered."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Dromaeosaurus albertensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dromaeosaurus"}]

name: Troodon
dietDetails: Small prey
discoveryHistory:
• A single tooth was discovered in 1856 by Ferdinand Vandeveer Hayden.
• Named by Joseph Leidy in 1856, making it one of the first dinosaurs named in North America.
• The genus has been considered a 'wastebasket taxon' due to confusing fossil fragments.
interestingFacts: ["Had one of the largest brain-to-body size ratios of any dinosaur.","Possessed large, forward-facing eyes, suggesting excellent nocturnal vision.","Its serrated teeth suggest an omnivorous diet."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Troodon formosus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troodon"}]

name: Gorgosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1913 by Charles M. Sternberg in Alberta, Canada.
• Named by Lawrence Lambe in 1914.
• Over 20 skeletons have been found, making it one of the best-represented tyrannosaurids.
interestingFacts: ["Coexisted with another tyrannosaurid, Daspletosaurus.","Had a lighter and more gracile build compared to T. rex.","Possessed a small horn-like crest in front of its eyes."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Gorgosaurus libratus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorgosaurus"}]

name: Daspletosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1921 by Charles Mortram Sternberg in Alberta.
• Dale Russell recognized it as a distinct genus and named it in 1970.
• Some specimens show bite marks from other tyrannosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["Was heavier and more robust than its contemporary, Gorgosaurus.","Considered by some scientists to be a direct ancestor of Tyrannosaurus rex.","Had proportionally larger teeth than T. rex."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Daspletosaurus torosus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daspletosaurus"}]

name: Styracosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• The first skull was collected in 1913 by Charles H. Sternberg in Alberta.
• Named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913.
• Bonebeds suggest it lived in massive herds.
interestingFacts: ["Characterized by a spectacular frill adorned with up to six long spikes.","Its nose horn could grow up to two feet long.","Despite its fearsome appearance, it was a strict herbivore."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Styracosaurus albertensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Styracosaurus"}]

name: Pachyrhinosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1946 by Charles M. Sternberg in Alberta, Canada.
• Described and named in 1950.
• The Pipestone Creek bonebed revealed hundreds of individuals.
interestingFacts: ["Lacked horns on its face, instead having massive bony bosses.","The bosses were likely used in head-butting combat.","Adapted to cold environments, with some fossils found near the Arctic Circle."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Pachyrhinosaurus lakustai description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pachyrhinosaurus"}]

name: Centrosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered by Lawrence Lambe in 1904 in Alberta, Canada.
• Lambe named the genus that same year based on incomplete remains.
• Enormous bonebeds in Dinosaur Provincial Park have yielded thousands of bones.
interestingFacts: ["Had a single large horn on its snout and small hornlets on its frill.","Lived in vast herds, potentially numbering in the thousands.","Many died in mass drowning events while crossing flooded rivers."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Centrosaurus apertus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrosaurus"}]

name: Chasmosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• First remains found in 1898 by Lawrence Lambe.
• Formally named by Lambe in 1914.
• Multiple species have been identified from the Dinosaur Park Formation.
interestingFacts: ["Its frill had massive openings (fenestrae) to reduce weight.","The frill was likely brightly colored for display purposes.","Possessed small brow horns compared to later relatives like Triceratops."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Chasmosaurus belli description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chasmosaurus"}]

name: Psittacosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1922 by the American Museum of Natural History expedition to Mongolia.
• Named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1923.
• Hundreds of complete skeletons have been found, making it one of the most studied dinosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["Preserved fossils reveal it had long quill-like bristles on its tail.","We know its exact color pattern due to fossilized melanosomes.","It swallowed stones (gastroliths) to help grind up tough plant matter."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Psittacosaurus mongoliensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psittacosaurus"}]

name: Pentaceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1921 by Charles H. Sternberg in the San Juan Basin, New Mexico.
• Named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1923.
• A massive skull was discovered in 1941, one of the largest of any terrestrial animal.
interestingFacts: ["Its name means 'five-horned face', including its two elongated cheek bones.","Has one of the largest skulls of any known land animal.","Lived further south than many of its northern ceratopsian relatives."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Pentaceratops sternbergii description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentaceratops"}]

name: Diabloceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• The first skull was found in 2002 by Don DeBlieux in Utah's Wahweap Formation.
• Described and named by James Kirkland and colleagues in 2010.
• Represents one of the oldest known centrosaurine ceratopsids.
interestingFacts: ["Named for the pair of devil-like horns curving up from the back of its frill.","Had a shorter, deeper snout than most other ceratopsians.","Helped prove that early ceratopsids diversified in southern Laramidia."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Diabloceratops eatoni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabloceratops"}]

name: Kosmoceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Found in 2006 by a volunteer in the Kaiparowits Formation of Utah.
• Formally named by Scott Sampson and colleagues in 2010.
• Its discovery shed light on dinosaur endemism in Late Cretaceous North America.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed 15 distinct horns or horn-like structures on its skull.","Its name translates to 'ornate horned face'.","The frill horns curled completely downward and forward."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Kosmoceratops richardsoni description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosmoceratops"}]

name: Zuniceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1996 by eight-year-old Christopher James Wolfe in New Mexico.
• Described and named by Douglas Wolfe and James Kirkland in 1998.
• Provides a crucial evolutionary link between earlier ceratopsians and later giants.
interestingFacts: ["The earliest known ceratopsian to feature true brow horns.","Lacked a solid frill, retaining a lighter, fenestrated structure.","Shows that large brow horns evolved before massive size in ceratopsians."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Zuniceratops christopheri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zuniceratops"}]

name: Sinoceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2008 in the Shandong province of China.
• Described by paleontologist Xu Xing and colleagues in 2010.
• The first ceratopsid dinosaur ever found outside of North America.
interestingFacts: ["Features a frill adorned with forward-curving hornlets.","Lacked brow horns, but had a prominent nasal horn.","Its presence in Asia challenged prior theories of ceratopsid migration."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Sinoceratops zhuchengensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinoceratops"}]

name: Einiosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1985 by Jack Horner in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana.
• Named by Scott Sampson in 1995.
• Found in low-diversity bonebeds, indicating it lived in herds.
interestingFacts: ["Distinctive for a prominent nasal horn that curved forward like a bottle opener.","Its name means 'buffalo lizard' in the Blackfoot language.","Only adults possessed the heavily curved horn; juveniles had straight ones."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Einiosaurus procurvicornis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einiosaurus"}]

name: Achelousaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1987 by a team led by Jack Horner in Montana.
• Named by Scott Sampson in 1995 alongside Einiosaurus.
• Represents an evolutionary transition between Einiosaurus and Pachyrhinosaurus.
interestingFacts: ["Had bony bosses on its snout and above its eyes instead of sharp horns.","Named after Achelous, a Greek river deity who had a horn torn off.","Fossils show a clear progression of horn loss within its lineage."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Achelousaurus horneri description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achelousaurus"}]

name: Nasutoceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2006 in the Kaiparowits Formation of Utah.
• Described by Scott Sampson and colleagues in 2013.
• Added to the growing list of unique dinosaurs from the region.
interestingFacts: ["Featured an unusually short, thick snout.","Possessed curved brow horns that resembled those of modern cattle.","Its deep snout indicates it ate tough, fibrous vegetation."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Nasutoceratops titusi description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasutoceratops"}]

name: Edmontosaurus
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• First remains were found in the late 19th century during the Bone Wars.
• Lawrence Lambe named the genus Edmontosaurus in 1917.
• Some of the best-preserved dinosaur mummies belong to this genus.
interestingFacts: ["Fossilized 'mummies' show detailed skin impressions and even a fleshy head comb.","Replaced its teeth continuously in a massive dental battery.","Was one of the main prey items for Tyrannosaurus rex."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Edmontosaurus annectens description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmontosaurus"}]

name: Corythosaurus
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1912 by Barnum Brown in Alberta, Canada.
• Named Corythosaurus by Brown in 1914.
• Early specimens featured extensive skin impressions.
interestingFacts: ["Its large, plate-like crest resembled a Corinthian helmet.","The crest was hollow and likely used for vocalization.","Lived alongside a vast diversity of other hadrosaurs."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Corythosaurus casuarius description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corythosaurus"}]

name: Maiasaura
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1978 by Marion Brandvold in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana.
• Jack Horner and Robert Makela named it Maiasaura in 1979.
• 'Egg Mountain' yielded nests, eggs, embryos, and juveniles.
interestingFacts: ["Provided the first solid evidence that dinosaurs cared for their young.","Hatchlings stayed in the nest and were fed by parents until they grew strong.","Lived in massive nesting colonies, much like modern seabirds."]
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Maiasaura peeblesorum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiasaura"}]

name: Tsintaosaurus
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1950 in Shandong Province, China.
• C.C. Young named the genus in 1958.
• Its distinctive crest was initially thought to be an artifact of preservation.

name: Rajasaurus narmadensis
dietDetails: Apex predator preying on large titanosaurian sauropods and ornithopods in Cretaceous floodplains.
discoveryHistory:
• Unearthed between 1981 and 1983 by Geological Survey of India (GSI) geologists G.N. Dwivedi and Dhananjay Mohabey near Rahioli, Gujarat.
• Excavated under the leadership of GSI paleontologist Suresh Srivastava, who recovered a nearly complete braincase and associated skeleton.
• Formally described in 2003 by a joint Indian-American team including Paul Sereno and Jeffrey A. Wilson after two decades in storage.
• Designated as the holotype GSI Type No. 19/999, providing crucial evidence of abelisaurid distribution on southern landmasses.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed a unique bony horn on its forehead formed by the fusion of its nasal and frontal bones, used potentially for display or head-butting.","Lived in a highly volcanic, lake-dotted floodplain environment that also served as a massive communal nesting ground for various dinosaur species.","Had extremely short, stubby arms and a robust neck, similar to other abelisaurids like Carnotaurus, suggesting it relied on its powerful jaws for hunting."]
sizeNotes: Consensus length of 6.6 to 7.4 meters and weight of 1.5 metric tonnes, standing about 2.4 meters tall at the hip.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Rajasaurus narmadensis description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajasaurus%20narmadensis"}]

name: Indosuchus
dietDetails: Carnivorous predator of small to medium-sized dinosaurs.
discoveryHistory:
• Collected between 1917 and 1919 by British geologist Charles Alfred Matley near Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh.
• Formally named by German paleontologist Friedrich von Huene in 1932.
• Described in detail by Huene and Matley in a joint monograph in 1933.
• Originally classified as an allosaurid, then a tyrannosaurid, before modern analysis confirmed it as an abelisaurid.
interestingFacts: ["Had a highly specialized narrow skull roof with frontals and parietals fused, forming a prominent crest.","Coexisted with other abelisaurids like Rajasaurus and Indosaurus, suggesting niche partitioning among Cretaceous Indian carnivores.","Its holotype specimen GSI K27/685 went missing from the GSI collections, making it a subject of taxonomic debate."]
sizeNotes: Estimated to be roughly 6 to 7 meters in length and weighing 1.2 metric tonnes.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Indosuchus raptorius description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indosuchus"}]

name: Vasuki
dietDetails: Ambush predator that subdued prey through constriction, likely feeding on early mammals, crocodilians, and turtles.
discoveryHistory:
• Holotype vertebrae GSI/GG/V/001–027 were originally discovered in 2005 at the Panandhro Lignite Mine in Kutch, Gujarat.
• The fossil material was initially misidentified as belonging to an extinct crocodilian and stored in the IIT Roorkee archives.
• Re-examined in 2024 by paleontologists Debajit Datta and Sunil Bajpai, who recognized it as a giant madtsoiid snake.
• Named after 'Vasuki', the mythical serpent king from Hindu cosmology, and 'indicus' to denote its geographic discovery site.
interestingFacts: ["Estimated to have reached a length of 10.9 to 15.2 meters (36 to 50 feet), rivaling the famous Paleocene Titanoboa for the title of the largest snake ever.","Had a very broad, cylindrical body and a heavy build, indicating it was a slow-moving ambush predator that lived in warm, marshy coastal swamps.","Lived during a period of global warming in the Eocene epoch, where high ambient temperatures enabled coldblooded ectotherms to reach such enormous sizes."]
sizeNotes: Length estimates range from 10.9 to 15.2 meters with a weight of approximately 1 metric tonne based on vertebral dimensions.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Vasuki indicus description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasuki"}]

name: Sivatherium
dietDetails: Browsed on leaves, shrubs, and woody vegetation.
discoveryHistory:
• First fossils discovered in the Siwalik Hills of northern India and described in 1836 by Hugh Falconer and Captain Proby Thomas Cautley.
• The bizarre skeletal remains initially sparked intense debate and were mistakenly likened to elephants, rhinos, or oxen.
• Re-examined in 2016 through a detailed 3D skeletal reconstruction using fossils housed at the Natural History Museum in London.
• Placed within the family Giraffidae, closely related to the modern okapi.
interestingFacts: ["One of the largest ruminant mammals that ever lived, standing over 2.2 meters tall at the shoulder.","Had a short, robust neck and sturdy limbs, differing from modern giraffes, and possessed a massive skull topped with large, palm-like ossicones.","Known to have coexisted with early human ancestors, as depicted in ancient rock art in Sahara regions, surviving until about 10,000 years ago."]
sizeNotes: Shoulder height of 2.2 meters, total length around 3 meters, and weight of approximately 1,246 kg.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Sivatherium giganteum description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sivatherium"}]

name: Stegodon ganesa
dietDetails: Browser feeding on grass, leaves, and twigs in Pleistocene river plains.
discoveryHistory:
• Formally described and named in 1846 by Hugh Falconer and Proby Thomas Cautley based on fossils found in the Siwalik Hills.
• Extensive skull and tusk material has been recovered across northern India, Pakistan, and Myanmar.
• Recent excavations in 2025 recovered exceptionally preserved fossils in the Chandrapur district of Maharashtra.
• These Maharashtra fossils were found in deep riverbed sediments and dated to approximately 25,000 years ago.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed enormous, nearly straight tusks that grew up to 4 meters in length, rivaling the animal's own body size.","The tusks were so closely spaced that the animal could not lower its trunk between them, likely resting it over them instead.","Coexisted with Pleistocene hominids and early humans in the Indian subcontinent, as evidenced by Paleolithic tools found nearby."]
sizeNotes: Shoulder height of up to 4 meters, and weight estimated at around 10 metric tonnes.
sources: [{"citation":"Paleobiology Database (PBDB) species record","url":"https://paleobiodb.org"},{"citation":"Stegodon ganesa description in paleontological literature","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stegodon%20ganesa"}]

name: Shringasaurus

name: Gigantophis garstini
dietDetails: Apex ambush predator preying on early basal proboscideans (such as Moeritherium) and primitive artiodactyls.

discoveryHistory:
• Skull acquired from illegal fossil dealers who had artificial plaster added to make it look complete.
